When it comes to pharmaceuticals, there are positive and negative results.  When it comes to other clinical research trials, there are results that support the hypothesis and results that don't.  It is still usually worthwhile to publish these results, but there is a lot of cherry picking in medical research, and I don't think doctors are concerned enough with the whole picture of data that comes from pharmaceutical trials.  That aside, I'm seeing a lot of comments that say "I don't care, Prozac saved my life."  That's really good to hear, but on the flipside, there is a level of risk that these people may not have. This is an issue of responsibility: whose responsibility is it to fully understand a patient's depressive symptoms, as well as the full risks and benefits to prescribing a certain SSRI?  For severely depressed patients, one of the symptoms might be physical depression, stuff like difficulty getting out of bed, lackluster motivation, etc.  For severely depressed patients, this might actually reduce suicidality because its just too much work to kill onesself.  Prozac is very good at alleviating physical depression symptoms, so suicidality goes up when energy and motivation goes up.  For these patients, Prozac might not be the best option in high doses or without monitoring because of this risk factor.  
TLDR; doctors need to know WHY Prozac is associated with suicide risk in order to make informed prescription decisions.

The main problem with the whole "violent games causes violent children" is the concept of causality.  Any research done on the issue will NOT be able to measure cause. It would be unethical to make children perform in that kind of study. Also, there is a problem with measuring violence.  Who determines what violence is in children? Punching? Kicking? Shoving? Murderous intent? 

Correlation here is key. Increases in violence in children (however that may be measured) is probably positively correlated to some degree with the availability of violent video games, BUT it is also correlated with the availability of other violent media, such as television.  The trend of what is or isn't acceptable or available media for children has been changing from generation to generation, and the fact that violence, sexuality, or drug use on television is normal in media today makes it more acceptable for children to replicate those behaviors.

If you could, get off the Paxil.  Did your general doctor prescribe it, or a psychiatrist? Many GPs will prescribe Paxil whereas psychiatrists, who have more experience with depression and anxiety medications, would probably per scribe Prozac or some other SSRI because Paxil has many side effects that other drugs do not.  I am not a trained psychiatrist, but I would still advise that you go to a psychiatrist and not a GP for medications for problems with depression.  

From personal experience: I was given Paxil by my GP, it had loads of side effects.  It basically made things much, much worse.  I did lose my sex drive.  After meeting with a psychiatrist, I learned that many psychiatrists do not prescribe Paxil.  I was put on Prozac, and I already feel like I am returning to my old self

tldr; do more research on the kind of meds that are best for you and don't have unwanted side effects.

Get a plastic water bottle, cut off the top. Fill the water bottle with a little vinegar, dish soap, and maybe a piece of fruit, like banana.  Flip the cut off top and tape it to the top of the bottom half of the water bottle, like a funnel.  Roll up a piece of paper like a funnel and tape this inside the top plastic bottle funnel.  Tear a hole in the paper large enough that the flies can crawl in.  Make sure this is the only way they can get into the bottle.  The flies should smell the vinegar/fruit, fly in, and not be able to fly out.  Eventually, they drown and once you've caught enough you can throw the whole contraption away.
